samples.text:
Nowadays many companies prefer to give workers short-term contracts instead of permanent jobs. This situation has some advantages but also many disadvantages for the workers, which I will discuss in this essay.

On the one hand, short-term contracts can be good for some workers. First of all, they give people more freedom. If a worker does not like the job or the company, he can simply leave when the contract finish and look for something better. Also, young people can try different jobs and get experience in many areas before they decide their career. For example, a graduate can work six months in marketing and then six months in sales. Moreover, some contracts pay a higher salary per hour because the company do not need to pay for holidays or pension.

On the other hand, the disadvantages are serious. The biggest problem is that there is no job security. Workers do not know if they will have a job next year, so it is difficult for them to plan the future, for example to buy a house or start a family. Banks also do not like to give loan to people without permanent job. In addition, temporary workers often do not receive the same benefits like sick pay, training or promotion. As a result, they may feel stressed and not part of the company.

In conclusion, short-term contracts give workers flexibility and the chance to gain different experiences, but they also create insecurity and fewer benefits. In my opinion, they are suitable for young people at the start of their career, but for most workers a permanent job is better.
samples.why: Covers advantages and disadvantages for workers · relevant ideas with simple examples but limited development · formulaic linking · adequate vocabulary · several errors in agreement, articles and prepositions that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
It is becoming increasingly common for employers to hire staff on fixed-term contracts instead of offering them permanent positions. For workers, this arrangement brings some genuine benefits, but in my view these are outweighed by the insecurity it creates for most people.

There are some advantages to short-term employment. Firstly, it offers flexibility, which suits certain groups such as students, parents returning to work or people who want to travel between contracts. Secondly, it allows workers to gain experience across a range of organisations and industries in a relatively short time, which can make their CV more attractive and help them discover what kind of work suits them best. In some sectors, such as information technology, skilled contractors are also able to charge higher rates than permanent staff because employers value their specialist knowledge.

However, for the majority of employees, the disadvantages are more significant. The lack of job security is the most serious issue, as workers cannot be sure whether their contract will be renewed. This uncertainty makes it difficult to make long-term commitments, such as taking out a mortgage or starting a family, and it can cause considerable stress. In addition, temporary staff are often excluded from benefits like paid holidays, sick leave and pension schemes, and they rarely receive the training or promotion opportunities which is offered to permanent colleagues. Because they know they may soon leave, they may also feel less loyal to the company and less valued by their managers.

In conclusion, short-term contracts can be attractive for highly skilled professionals and for people who want flexibility at a particular stage of life. For most workers, though, the loss of security, benefits and career development makes this type of employment a less desirable option than a permanent job.
samples.why: Both sides addressed with a clear overall view · ideas extended and supported with relevant examples · logical paragraphing and linking · good range of vocabulary (job security, fixed-term) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The shift away from permanent employment towards fixed-term and project-based contracts has reshaped working life in many economies. For employees, this change offers a certain degree of freedom, but it also transfers much of the risk that employers once carried onto individual workers.

On the positive side, short-term contracts can suit people whose priorities do not fit a conventional career path. A recent graduate, for example, may use a series of placements to sample different industries before committing to one, while a parent may value the ability to work intensively for several months and then take time off. For those with scarce, in-demand skills, contract work can be financially rewarding, as employers are often willing to pay a premium for expertise they need only temporarily. Moving between organisations also broadens professional networks and exposes workers to a variety of practices, which can make them more adaptable.

The drawbacks, however, fall most heavily on those with the least bargaining power. Without the assurance of continued employment, workers find it hard to plan ahead: securing a mortgage, supporting dependants or even booking a holiday becomes a gamble when income may stop within months. Temporary staff frequently miss out on entitlements such as sick pay, pension contributions and parental leave, and employers have little incentive to invest in training someone who may soon leave. Over time, this can trap people in a cycle of insecure jobs with limited prospects for promotion. The psychological toll should not be overlooked either, as persistent uncertainty is a well-known source of stress.

To sum up, short-term contracts can offer flexibility, variety and, for skilled professionals, higher earnings. For the majority of workers, however, these advantages come at the price of financial insecurity, reduced benefits and weaker career development, which is why such arrangements work best when they are genuinely chosen rather than imposed.
samples.why: Fully addresses advantages and disadvantages for workers with insightful, well-supported ideas · clear progression · cohesion managed skilfully · wide, precise vocabulary (bargaining power, entitlements) · wide range of error-free structures.
